The [EDA page](eda.qmd) shows *what* we found in the data. This page shows *what we did about it*. Each fix is
numbered, has evidence behind it, and is logged in a GitHub issue or decision record, so the path from raw data to
prediction can be audited.

::: {.callout-note}
## Only aggregates are shown
As on the EDA page, every number and chart here comes from summary tables, never from policy or claim rows
(competition rules, section 5b).
:::

## The pipeline at a glance

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Raw tables<br/>policies x3, claims,<br/>customers, addresses,<br/>weather"] --> B["Cleaning rules<br/>R1-R6 / D-01-D-27"]
  B --> C["Joins<br/>customer, address,<br/>weather-year"]
  B --> D["Claims clean<br/>dedupe, exclude declined<br/>and out-of-period"]
  D --> E["Develop to ultimate<br/>chain ladder by peril,<br/>BF for slow perils"]
  E --> F["Split small / large<br/>at 50,000"]
  C --> G["Features<br/>bands, splines,<br/>missing levels, log SI"]
  F --> H["Model frame<br/>one row per policy-year"]
  G --> H
  H --> I["GLMs per line<br/>+ trend + offset"]
```

## 1. Cleaning rules

Cian set up the rules framework early in the project. Each rule has an ID, the evidence, an action, and audit tables
for every changed cell, exclusion and flag (`notebooks/01b_corrections`). Gerard reproduced the rules in SQL, added
more from his final review, and numbered the decisions D-01 to D-39 (`audit/DECISIONS.md`).

| Rule | Field | Problem | Fix | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 / D-19 | motor `customer_id` | Leading zeros lost: 10% of motor rows match no customer | Left-pad to 8 characters | #51 |
| R2 / D-01 | `exposure` (all lines) | Some rows in days (up to 365) or on a 360-day year | Recompute as (end - start + 1) / 365 | #52 |
| R3 / D-02 | home `sum_insured` | About 0.2% of rows 1,000x too large | Divide by 1,000 at 1m or more (contents), 10m or more (buildings) | #53 |
| R4 / D-24 | buildings `construction_type` | Mixed case; timber `T` to 2022, `W` from 2023 | Lower-case and trim; merge as `timber` | #54 |
| R5 / D-19 | claims | 604 duplicates, identical apart from the ID | Keep one copy | #55 |
| R6 / D-03 | claims | Declined claims, and losses outside any policy period | Exclude from the target | #56 |
| D-26 | `elevation_m`, region R11 | Recorded in feet (3.28x every other region) | Divide by 3.28084 | #154 |
| D-27 | `year_built` = 1900 | Placeholder on 19,014 addresses | Typical year built for the energy rating | #155 |
| D-04 | `customer_service_contacts` | Leaks the outcome (claimants 3.0 vs 0.4) | Excluded from every model | |
| D-05 | `written_premium` | Annual on every row, and adds nothing beyond the risk factors | Excluded as a feature; earned premium used for loss ratios | |

## 2. Building the target

The competition asks for the **expected ultimate cost** of each 2025 policy row. The training target has to mean the
same thing, so each claim goes through four steps.

**Step 1: clean the claims.** For contents, every claim is accounted for, from the raw table to the target total:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(recon.filter(d => d.step <= 5).map(d => ({step: d.step, "": d.description, claims: d.n_claims, "net cost": d.net_cost})),
  {format: {claims: fmt, "net cost": d => fmt(Math.round(d))}})
```

```{ojs}
md`The check row confirms the target total on the policy rows is exactly the cleaned claims total
(${fmt(Math.round(recon.find(d => d.step === 6).net_cost))}). Nothing is lost or double-counted in the join.`
```

**Step 2: net cost.** Incurred to date (already net of the excess) minus recoveries. Motor recoveries are about 6% of
incurred; home lines have none.

**Step 3: develop to ultimate.** Claims valued at 31 December 2024 are not all reported or settled yet. Each claim is
grossed up by the inverse of its peril's reported share at its age:

$$
\text{ultimate}_k \;=\; \text{net cost}_k \times \frac{1}{F_{\text{peril}}(\text{age}_k)},
\qquad
F(l) \;=\; \prod_{m>l}\left(1 - \frac{d_m}{n_m}\right)
$$

$F$ is a right-truncated product-limit estimate of the cost-weighted reporting pattern. For the two slow perils
(buildings subsidence and motor bodily injury), the 2024 loss year uses **Bornhuetter-Ferguson** instead, because the
chain ladder over-reacted in the backtest (×1.18 and ×1.33 of actual) while BF was close (×1.01 and ×1.13).
Alan's [chain-ladder notebook](https://github.com/almac09/iaa-hackathon-2026/blob/main/workings/chainladder.ipynb)
cross-checked the development with Mack and bootstrap methods.

**Step 4: split small and large.** Claims above **50,000** go to a separate large-claim model in buildings and motor
(see [How our GLM works](our-glm.qmd)). Contents is modelled without a split.

## 3. Feature engineering

### Exposure and premium

* **Exposure** is always (end - start + 1) / 365. It enters every model as an **offset**, $\log e_i$, so a half-year
  policy costs half as much, other things equal.
* **Earned premium** = written premium × exposure. It is used for loss ratios only, never as a rating factor.
* **Line from the policy number**: the first letter of `policy_id` (B, C, M) gives the line (Alan, #12).

### How each kind of factor enters the model

| Kind | What it does | Example in our model |
|---|---|---|
| **Categorical** | One coefficient per level; the base level is 0 | cover type, tenure, customer segment |
| **Grouped / capped** | Rare high values pooled | prior claims and missed payments: 3 or more becomes one level |
| **Band** | A numeric cut into intervals | motor prior claims (0 / 1 / 2+), large-claim NCB bands |
| **Spline** | A smooth curve for a numeric factor, built from cubic pieces | elevation, distance to river, NCB years, vehicle age |
| **Missing level** | Its own coefficient where data is missing | contents: missing flood zone ×1.73, unknown distance to river |
| **Log transform** | An elasticity on a size measure | contents: $0.777 \times \log(\text{sum insured})$ |
| **Trend** | Calendar-year slope, carried to 2025 | +4.3% a year for contents, +3.7% for motor |

The final rating factors in the model behind the [calculator](underwriting-calculator.qmd):

```{ojs}
featureRows = Object.entries(model.lines).flatMap(([line, L]) => Object.entries(L.components).flatMap(([comp, C]) =>
  C.terms.map(t => ({
    line, component: comp === "small" ? "small claims" : "large claims",
    factor: L.inputs[t.input]?.label ?? t.term,
    kind: t.kind === "log_si" ? "log transform" : t.kind,
    levels: t.kind === "categorical" ? Object.keys(t.levels).length : t.kind === "band" ? t.bands.length : t.kind === "spline" ? `${t.pieces.length - 2} cubic pieces` : "1 coefficient",
    "unknown allowed": t.kind === "spline" ? (L.inputs[t.input]?.allow_missing ? "yes" : "no") : t.kind === "categorical" ? ("MISSING" in t.levels ? "yes" : "no") : t.kind === "band" ? (t.missing ? "yes" : "no") : "no"
  }))
))
```

```{ojs}
viewof featLine = Inputs.radio(["contents", "motor"], {label: "Line", value: "contents"})
```

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(featureRows.filter(d => d.line === featLine), {columns: ["component", "factor", "kind", "levels", "unknown allowed"], rows: 25})
```

### What we deliberately left out

* **Leakage:** customer service contacts, renewal decision, written premium.
* **Not available in the emerging market (D-31):** region, occupation, credit band, exact ages, annual mileage and
  telematics. The model uses the age bands both markets share.
* **Governance:** previous insurer, branch, campaign code and marketing-only fields were reviewed for proxy and
  fairness risk (Bridget's issue #38 on ethics and proxy variables, and Alan's GLM governance notes).

## 4. Missing values

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(missing.map(d => ({table: d.src, field: d.column_name, missing: d.n_missing, rows: d.n_rows, share: d.n_missing / d.n_rows})),
  {format: {missing: fmt, rows: fmt, share: d3.format(".1%")}})
```

The rule (D-06): **missing is information, not noise.** In the developed market a missing flood zone has a relativity of
1.71, so it gets its own level rather than an imputed value. Smoothed numeric factors get a missing indicator in place of
the curve. In the emerging market about 12% of each field is missing. Gerard tested filling the gaps against keeping
them as their own level, scored out of time in both directions. Filling didn't pass, so the missing levels stayed.
